screens.title: A systematic troubleshooting approach
screens.narratorSegment: When you face a network problem, a methodical approach saves time and avoids corrective actions that make things worse. Begin by verifying basic connectivity: can the instance reach an IP or hostname, and do simple utilities like ping and traceroute behave as expected? These initial checks rule out local misconfiguration and show whether a packet leaves the host. Next, inspect VPC Flow Logs to see whether traffic is being allowed or denied, and whether the firewall or routing layer is the reported blocker. If flow logs show denial, you have direct evidence to repair firewall rules. If flows are allowed but traffic still fails, use Network Intelligence Center’s Connectivity Tests to simulate a full path and reveal which configuration element prevents successful transit. After you identify the probable cause, validate service-level settings such as load balancer health checks or Cloud NAT allocation. A common misconception is to assume the application is broken first; instead, use these steps to gather evidence and reach a confident fix. Which single check would you run first during an outage, and why? A systematic troubleshooting approach means start with reachability, then inspect logs, then simulate paths—each step narrows the hypothesis space.. In practical terms, how to structure your investigation so you find the true cause. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › Systematic troubleshooting
Definition

A stepwise diagnostic workflow

A reproducible pattern: verify reachability, inspect flows, simulate paths, then validate service configuration. Each step provides different evidence types useful for root cause analysis.

1
Verify basic connectivity
Use ping and traceroute to confirm packets are leaving and where they stop.
2
Inspect VPC Flow Logs
Confirm if the network allowed or denied traffic and identify the reporter.
3
Simulate packet paths
Connectivity Tests show the configuration element blocking the path.
Concrete example
Instance cannot reach another instance

Confirm with ping. If ping fails, check flow logs for jsonPayload.connection.is_allowed=false and reporter="FIREWALL" to show a firewall denial. Then run a Connectivity Test to confirm which firewall rule blocks the path.

Common misconception
People often assume application logic is broken first. Evidence from flow logs or connectivity simulation frequently points to network configuration as the true cause.
Key Takeaway

A structured, evidence-driven approach is faster and less disruptive than ad-hoc fixes.

screens.title: Basic connectivity checks
screens.narratorSegment: Basic connectivity checks are your first line of defense and give quick evidence about whether packets can travel between endpoints. Use ping to verify simple ICMP reachability and traceroute to see the hop-by-hop path and where it stops. These tools don't tell you why a packet was blocked — only that it did or did not arrive — but they are essential to form an initial hypothesis. For example, if ping from a VM to another internal IP fails, that indicates either a network block or the destination not listening for ICMP. A traceroute that stops at the first gateway suggests routing or firewall rules close to the source. A common error is to assume traceroute always reveals the exact firewall rule; it shows where traffic stops but not the specific rule. Combine traceroute with flow logs to find whether the flow was denied and which rule reported the denial. Practice: run ping and traceroute first, then follow the evidence to logs or simulation tools. How would traceroute results change your next diagnostic step? Basic connectivity checks means use them to form the first hypothesis; they must be combined with logs to identify the blocking rule.. In practical terms, when to use ping and traceroute, and what they prove. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › Basic connectivity
When to use

Quick reachability checks

Ping and traceroute validate whether traffic leaves a host and the path it takes. They are fast and often run from the VM itself during incident triage.

Commands (examples)
ping 10.128.1.2
traceroute 10.128.1.2
  • Ping confirms ICMP reachability; a failure is evidence but not cause.
  • Traceroute shows hops and where traffic stops; combine with logs to identify blocks.
  • Both are subject to filtering — lack of response can be intentional.
Concrete scenario
ICMP blocked between VMs

If ping from instance-a to instance-b times out, try traceroute. If traceroute halts before the destination, check for firewall egress rules on the source subnet or ingress rules on the destination subnet.

Misconception
Assuming a failed ping equals application failure is wrong. Ping tests only indicate network reachability for ICMP, not application-layer readiness.
Key Takeaway

Use ping and traceroute to form the initial hypothesis, then validate with logs and simulation.

screens.title: VPC Flow Logs
screens.narratorSegment: VPC Flow Logs are structured records of network flows to and from VM instances. They include source and destination IPs, ports, protocol, and whether the flow was allowed. Enable flow logs at the subnet level and then query them in Cloud Logging or export to BigQuery for deeper analysis. A typical use case is to search for denied flows between two internal IPs. For example, a Cloud Logging query filtering resource. type to the subnet and matching src and dest IPs, protocol, and is_allowed=false will reveal firewall blocks and include the reporter field showing which subsystem flagged the denial. A common misconception is that flow logs capture every packet; they sample flows and are best for pattern analysis and confirmation, not packet-level debugging. Use them to identify unexpected traffic patterns, blocked connections, or attempts to reach non-existent services. When you find a denied flow, the logs give you the evidence to change or remove a specific firewall rule safely. Which log field would you check first to prove a firewall denial? VPC Flow Logs means use flow records to confirm whether traffic was allowed or denied and to identify the reporter responsible for the decision.. In practical terms, capture and query flow records to find denied connections. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › VPC Flow Logs
What they are

Structured records of network flows

Flow logs include src/dest IP and port, protocol, whether the flow was allowed, and a reporter field that often shows FIREWALL when a rule denied the flow.

Sample Cloud Logging filter
resource.type="gce_subnetwork"
jsonPayload.connection.src_ip="10.128.0.5"
jsonPayload.connection.dest_ip="10.128.0.6"
jsonPayload.connection.is_allowed=false
  • Enable at the subnet level; consider exporting to BigQuery for complex queries.
  • Look for is_allowed=false and reporter="FIREWALL" to prove a firewall denial.
  • Use timestamps and tags to correlate with incident windows.
Concrete example
Denied internal connection

A flow log entry showing is_allowed=false between two internal IPs points directly to a firewall rule. The reporter field often indicates where the decision occurred.

Misconception
Flow logs are sampled and not packet-by-packet captures. They are for pattern and configuration analysis, not raw packet debugging.
Key Takeaway

Use flow logs to gather conclusive evidence of allowed or denied traffic before changing network rules.

screens.title: Network Intelligence Center
screens.narratorSegment: Network Intelligence Center bundles tools that help you reason about network configuration without manually scanning every rule. Connectivity Tests lets you simulate a packet from source to destination and it inspects firewall rules, routes, and other configuration to say if the connection should succeed. This is invaluable when you need to answer "why can't my VM talk to X?" Network Topology provides a visual map of resources and traffic flows so you can spot unexpected paths or dependencies. Firewall Insights analyzes your rules to find shadow rules or overly permissive settings. A concrete example: run a Connectivity Test from a VM to a load balancer IP; the test will surface a firewall rule blocking the probe if one exists. A common pitfall is over-relying on topology visuals without verifying current flow state — always follow visual inspection with flow logs or connectivity test results. After using these tools you should be able to point to the exact config element causing failure and produce a targeted fix. What evidence from a connectivity test would you record to support a change request?

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › Network Intelligence Center
Toolset overview

Connectivity Tests and Topology

Connectivity Tests simulates packet flow and identifies the configuration element blocking it. Network Topology draws relationships between resources and traffic flows. Firewall Insights finds shadow and overly broad rules.

  • Connectivity Tests analyze firewall rules, routes, and tags to predict success.
  • Topology helps reveal unexpected resource paths and dependencies.
  • Firewall Insights highlights rules that never match or which are too permissive.
Concrete example
Blocked probe identified by Connectivity Test

A test from a VM to a load balancer will report which firewall rule or route prevents the connection. It provides the exact match and the reason, which is actionable evidence for a fix.

Misconception
Topology is not a live packet trace. Use it to form hypotheses, then confirm with flow logs or connectivity tests that evaluate live configuration state.
Key Takeaway

Use simulation and visualization together to convert configuration complexity into precise, actionable evidence.

screens.title: Debugging Private Google Access and Cloud NAT
screens.narratorSegment: Instances without external IP addresses rely on Private Google Access to reach Google APIs and Cloud NAT to reach the public internet. Private Google Access allows internal-only VMs to contact Google APIs using internal routes; Cloud NAT provides source address translation so private instances can initiate outbound internet connections. If a private VM cannot reach a Google A P I, verify that Private Google Access is enabled on the subnet and that DNS resolves to the private googleapis domain when required. Also check for egress firewall rules that might block internal egress to Google’s IP ranges. If a VM fails to reach the public internet, check that Cloud NAT is configured for the correct subnet and region, that enough NAT IPs are allocated, and that egress firewall rules allow traffic from the NAT gateway. A common mistake is confusing Private Google Access and Cloud NAT: Private Google Access does not provide access to third-party APIs. When you troubleshoot, ask whether the destination is a Google A P I or an external service; that determines whether to inspect Private Google Access or Cloud NAT first.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › Private Google Access vs Cloud NAT
Feature comparison
Private Google Access
Allows instances without external IPs to reach Google APIs via internal routes. Check subnet-level setting and DNS domain resolution.
Cloud NAT
Provides NAT for outbound internet connections. Verify correct subnet mapping, NAT IP allocation, and egress firewall rules.
Troubleshooting checklist
  • Is Private Google Access enabled on the subnet for Google APIs?
  • Does DNS resolve private.googleapis.com or restricted.googleapis.com if required?
  • Is Cloud NAT configured for the correct subnet and region?
  • Are there enough NAT IP addresses allocated?
  • Do firewall egress rules allow traffic from the NAT gateway or internal instances?
Misconception: Private Google Access does not provide access to third-party APIs. If you need external API access from a private instance, Cloud NAT is the correct feature to inspect first.
Key Takeaway

Identify whether the destination is a Google API or the public internet, then inspect Private Google Access or Cloud NAT respectively.

screens.title: Firewall troubleshooting and common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Firewall rules are a frequent source of connectivity failure. On Google Cloud, firewall rules have direction, priority, and match criteria. A common problem is an egress rule unintentionally denying traffic by destination range or a priority that causes a deny rule to take precedence. Shadow rules are rules that never match because a higher-priority rule already handles the traffic; Firewall Insights can help you find these. Another common mistake is blocking health check probes — load balancer health checks originate from Google-owned IP ranges and must be allowed to the backend instance port. When investigating, check rule direction (ingress vs egress), source and destination ranges, protocols and ports, and the rule priority. Use VPC Flow Logs to confirm which rule reported the denial. A useful exercise is to intentionally block ICMP from one instance to another and then verify the flow log entries and the Connectivity Test result that points to the specific rule. What firewall field will you examine first to confirm rule direction? Firewall troubleshooting and common mistakes means check direction, priority, match ranges, and reporters; use flow logs and firewall insights to find shadowed or blocking rules.. In practical terms, find shadow rules, priority issues, and mismatched directions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Firewall rules need careful review

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › Firewall troubleshooting
Key checks
Inspect these rule attributes carefully:
  • Direction: ingress or egress.
  • Priority: lower value wins.
  • Source and destination IP ranges and tags.
  • Protocol and port matches.
Use VPC Flow Logs
Look for is_allowed=false and reporter="FIREWALL" entries to see the denying rule and timestamp evidence for audits.
Concrete scenario
ICMP blocked by a high-priority egress deny

If a deny rule with higher priority targets your source tag and destination range, lower-priority allow rules won't apply. Deleting or adjusting the deny rule resolves the block. Confirm with Connectivity Test and flow logs.

Pitfall: forgetting to allow health check IP ranges will cause load balancer backends to appear unhealthy. Always verify firewall rules permit probes from Google's health check ranges to the expected port.
Key Takeaway

Firewall debugging needs evidence from logs and tests; adjust priority and directions carefully to avoid unintentional denial.

screens.title: Load balancer troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Load balancing problems often present as intermittent failures or capacity-related errors, but the root cause is frequently configuration: incorrect health check paths, wrong port mappings, or firewalls blocking health probes. Health checks must match what the application responds to; if your app reports healthy only on "/healthz" but the health check uses "/", the probe will fail and the backend will be removed from rotation. Check backend instance groups and port mappings to ensure requested ports match what the service listens on. Also confirm firewall rules permit health check probes from Google's IP ranges to reach the backend port. Cloud Load Balancing logs are useful to see request distribution and backend errors; correlate log entries with health status to diagnose whether the problem is the backend itself or the load balancer configuration. A common misconception is that increasing capacity solves intermittent errors; first inspect health checks and logs to find whether backends were unhealthy or misconfigured. After fixing probes or firewall rules, validate by reviewing health status and re-running Connectivity Tests if needed. Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › Load balancer troubleshooting
Health checks

Probe path, port, and protocol must match

If health checks fail, the load balancer will stop sending requests to that backend. Verify the probe path and port are correct and that the application returns success on that path.

Checklist
  • Health check path and port match the application.
  • Backend instance groups include correct instances and ports.
  • Firewall rules allow probes from Google health check ranges.
  • Use load balancer logs to correlate errors with backend selection.
Concrete example
Backends removed due to wrong probe path

If your app only serves status on "/healthz" but the health check uses "/", probes will fail. Fix the probe path, then check backend health and logs to confirm requests resume normally.

Misconception: scaling backends will not help if health checks are misconfigured. Address probe mismatch first to restore healthy endpoints.
Key Takeaway

Confirm probe configuration and firewall allowances before adjusting capacity or instance groups.

screens.title: Connectivity Tests in practice
screens.narratorSegment: Connectivity Tests simulate a packet’s path between two endpoints and can identify which configuration element blocks traffic. keyIdea.text: Run a Connectivity Test with correct source, destination, and protocol to surface the blocking rule and its reason.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › Connectivity Tests
Steps
  1. Choose Source: resource or IP (e.g., Compute Engine instance-a).
  2. Choose Destination: IP or resource (e.g., 10.128.1.2).
  3. Select Protocol: ICMP, TCP, or UDP; start the test.
  4. Review the result for the exact rule or route blocking the connection.
Record the test configuration and result: source identity, destination IP, protocol, timestamp, and the named blocking rule. This makes remediation auditable and reproducible.
Concrete example
ICMP blocked: test shows deny rule

A test from instance-a to 10.128.1.2 using ICMP will typically show the deny rule that matches source tag, destination range, and protocol. Use that named rule to guide deletion or modification.

Misconception: a connectivity test prediction is a substitute for logs. Always confirm predicted denial with VPC Flow Logs when possible to capture runtime evidence.
Key Takeaway

Connectivity Tests produce the actionable name of the blocking rule; pair that with flow logs before making changes.

screens.title: Lab walkthrough: diagnose blocked ICMP between two VMs
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough guides you through a real diagnostic sequence. First, provision two Compute Engine VMs in the same VPC but different subnets, tagging them so firewall rules can target them. Next, create a firewall rule that intentionally denies ICMP egress from instance-a to instance-b’s IP. SSH into instance-a and run ping to verify failure, then run a Connectivity Test from the console with instance-a as source and instance-b’s IP as destination using ICMP. The test will identify the deny rule. If flow logs were enabled, query Cloud Logging filtering the subnet resource type, the source and destination IPs, and protocol equal to 1 for ICMP; look for entries where is_allowed=false and reporter="FIREWALL". Finally, remove the blocking firewall rule and re-run the ping and Connectivity Test to confirm connectivity is restored. This sequence teaches you to combine SSH checks, simulated tests, and logs to prove the cause and validate the fix. After completing it, reflect on which step gave you the most conclusive evidence. content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › Lab: blocked ICMP
Step-by-step commands
gcloud compute instances create instance-a --zone=us-central1-a --machine-type=e2-micro --image-family=debian-11 --image-project=debian-cloud --tags=instance-a-tag

gcloud compute instances create instance-b --zone=us-central1-a --machine-type=e2-micro --image-family=debian-11 --image-project=debian-cloud --tags=instance-b-tag

gcloud compute firewall-rules create block-icmp-a-to-b \
  --network=default \
  --action=DENY \
  --direction=EGRESS \
  --rules=icmp \
  --priority=1000 \
  --destination-ranges=10.128.1.2/32 \
  --source-tags=instance-a-tag
SSH into instance-a and run ping to verify failure. Then create a Connectivity Test from the Network Intelligence Center with source set to instance-a and destination to 10.128.1.2 using ICMP. The test will report the blocking firewall rule.
Inspect logs
If VPC Flow Logs are enabled, query Cloud Logging with:
resource.type="gce_subnetwork" AND jsonPayload.connection.src_ip="10.128.0.2" AND jsonPayload.connection.dest_ip="10.128.1.2" AND jsonPayload.connection.protocol=1
Look for entries where jsonPayload.connection.is_allowed=false and jsonPayload.reporter="FIREWALL" to confirm the deny and its timestamp. Then delete the firewall rule with the provided gcloud command and re-run your connectivity checks to validate the resolution.

Which single evidence item would you include in a remediation ticket to justify changing the firewall rule?

fullNarratorScript:
Network problems in cloud environments often look like timeouts, intermittent failures, or strange routing behavior. In this lesson you will learn a practical, repeatable approach: verify basic connectivity, inspect traffic with VPC Flow Logs, simulate packet paths with Connectivity Tests, and check service-specific features like Private Google Access and Cloud NAT. You will see concrete examples such as using ping and traceroute to confirm reachability, querying flow logs to find denied connections, and running a connectivity test that identifies a blocking firewall rule. I will also highlight common traps — for example, assuming cloud services behave like on-prem networks, or expecting Private Google Access to reach third-party APIs. By the end you will be able to pick the right tool for each stage of troubleshooting and verify a fix. Think about a recent connectivity outage you’ve seen: which of these tools would help you prove whether the network or the application caused the failure?

These objectives focus on practical skills you will need to diagnose cloud networking issues. First, you will learn to identify common network problems such as firewall misconfigurations, routing errors, and DNS failures. Recognizing these quickly narrows the investigation. Second, you will use VPC Flow Logs to analyze traffic records. That skill helps you confirm whether connections are being allowed or denied and to find unexpected traffic patterns. Third, you will practice using Network Intelligence Center tools: Connectivity Tests and Network Topology. These let you simulate packet paths and visualize relationships among resources which often reveal hidden dependencies. Finally, you will debug Private Google Access and Cloud NAT for instances without external IPs so your services can reach Google APIs and the public internet. Each objective is practical: they map directly to commands, console actions, and log queries you can run during an outage. As you practice, focus on what evidence each tool provides and how that evidence changes your hypothesis. Which tool would you pick first for a single failed connection?

These additional objectives build on the first set and focus on practical incident tasks you will perform under pressure. First, learn to interpret Network Topology and Firewall Insights to find shadow or overly permissive rules that affect traffic flow. That reduces false leads during an incident. Second, practice checking load balancer health checks and backend service mappings so you can diagnose intermittent service failures caused by misconfigured probes or wrong ports. Third, learn to read Cloud Load Balancing logs and health status to correlate client errors with backend failures. Finally, integrate these tools into a systematic workflow: quick reachability checks, flow inspection, simulation, then service-level checks. This workflow helps you avoid jumping to conclusions, such as blaming an application when a firewall denied the traffic. As you work, ask: which evidence would convince you to change a firewall or load balancer configuration?

When you face a network problem, a methodical approach saves time and avoids corrective actions that make things worse. Begin by verifying basic connectivity: can the instance reach an IP or hostname, and do simple utilities like ping and traceroute behave as expected? These initial checks rule out local misconfiguration and show whether a packet leaves the host. Next, inspect VPC Flow Logs to see whether traffic is being allowed or denied, and whether the firewall or routing layer is the reported blocker. If flow logs show denial, you have direct evidence to repair firewall rules. If flows are allowed but traffic still fails, use Network Intelligence Center’s Connectivity Tests to simulate a full path and reveal which configuration element prevents successful transit. After you identify the probable cause, validate service-level settings such as load balancer health checks or Cloud NAT allocation. A common misconception is to assume the application is broken first; instead, use these steps to gather evidence and reach a confident fix. Which single check would you run first during an outage, and why? A systematic troubleshooting approach means start with reachability, then inspect logs, then simulate paths—each step narrows the hypothesis space.. In practical terms, how to structure your investigation so you find the true cause. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Basic connectivity checks are your first line of defense and give quick evidence about whether packets can travel between endpoints. Use ping to verify simple ICMP reachability and traceroute to see the hop-by-hop path and where it stops. These tools don't tell you why a packet was blocked — only that it did or did not arrive — but they are essential to form an initial hypothesis. For example, if ping from a VM to another internal IP fails, that indicates either a network block or the destination not listening for ICMP. A traceroute that stops at the first gateway suggests routing or firewall rules close to the source. A common error is to assume traceroute always reveals the exact firewall rule; it shows where traffic stops but not the specific rule. Combine traceroute with flow logs to find whether the flow was denied and which rule reported the denial. VPC Flow Logs are structured records of network flows to and from VM instances. They include source and destination IPs, ports, protocol, and whether the flow was allowed. Instances without external IP addresses rely on Private Google Access to reach Google APIs and Cloud NAT to reach the public internet.
